
## 1. Background

*S. aureus* takes up the amino acid L-cystine with the ABC transporter **TcyABC**
(TcyA = substrate-binding protein, TcyB = permease, TcyC = ATPase; one operon, *tcyABC*).

In **Schwyter et al. 2025, *mSystems*** (doi:10.1128/msystems.00262-25) JE2 was evolved
in medium containing cell-free, sterile-filtered spent medium of *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*
PAO1 ("PA supernatant", PASN). *S. aureus* never met living *P. aeruginosa*: it only
sees the molecules *P. aeruginosa* secreted (e.g. HQNO, PQS, pyocyanin, siderophores,
proteases) – and a medium that is partly depleted of nutrients. An evolved isolate carried a
frameshift in *tcyA*; in its proteome TcyA was almost gone (log2FC −5.95 vs the
ancestor) and TcyB was reduced (−2.86), probably a polar effect. A non-functional
transporter gave partial protection against toxic compounds from *P. aeruginosa*
(selenocystine, PQS) – presumably because they enter the cell through TcyABC.

This leads to an idea: *maybe the ancestor already down-regulates TcyABC when it
is exposed to PASN – a fast, plastic version of what evolution did genetically?*

* **H1 (your hypothesis):** in the ancestor (anc), TcyA/B/C abundance is ______ in SN than in TSB.
* **H0 (null hypothesis):** ______
* **Which contrast tests this, and which sign of `diff` would support H1?**

```{r sign-rule}
explain_contrast("TSB_vs_SN_at_anc")
```

> *Your answer:* …

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check your formulation (open after you wrote yours)
H0: mean log2 abundance in anc_SN = anc_TSB. H1 (one-sided): lower in anc_SN.
With contrast `TSB_vs_SN_at_anc` (= TSB − SN), H1 predicts **diff > 0**.
Also decide now how large a change you would call *biologically relevant*
(e.g. |log2FC| > 1 = two-fold?). Deciding afterwards is cheating yourself.
:::

## 3. Find the three proteins

Gene names are empty in this data set. We search by **locus tag** (JE2 genome CP020619.1).

```{r find}
tcy <- find_protein(c("B7H15_13375", "B7H15_13370", "B7H15_13365")) |>
  select(protein_key, locus_tag, product, protein_id, staa8_uniprot, location) |>
  mutate(short_name = c(B7H15_13375 = "TcyA", B7H15_13370 = "TcyB",
                        B7H15_13365 = "TcyC")[locus_tag])
tcy
```

**Question:** the products are just called "amino acid ABC transporter …". How can
you convince yourself these really are TcyA/B/C? (Hint: `staa8_uniprot` →
look up the NCTC8325 ortholog on uniprot.org; check the location on the genome.)

There may be more than one way into the cell for cystine:

```{r find-cystine}
find_protein("cystine") |> select(locus_tag, product, protein_id, staa8_uniprot)
```

## 5. What does the prolfquapp DEA say?

```{r dea}
dea <- read_dea("total")
tcy_dea <- dea |>
  filter(locus_tag %in% tcy$locus_tag,
         contrast %in% c("TSB_vs_SN_at_anc", "TSB_vs_SN_at_stk", "TSB_vs_SN_at_stp",
                         "TSB_vs_SNpulse_at_anc")) |>
  left_join(select(tcy, locus_tag, short_name), by = "locus_tag") |>
  transmute(short_name, contrast, diff = round(diff, 2),
            fold_change = round(2^diff, 2), conf.low = round(conf.low, 2),
            conf.high = round(conf.high, 2), FDR = signif(FDR, 2), estimate_type) |>
  arrange(short_name, contrast)
tcy_dea
```

Translate the sign into words for TcyA in the ancestor:

```{r in-words}
tcyA_anc <- filter(tcy_dea, short_name == "TcyA", contrast == "TSB_vs_SN_at_anc")
sprintf("TcyA, anc: diff = %.2f -> TcyA is %s in TSB than in SN (factor %.2f)",
        tcyA_anc$diff, if_else(tcyA_anc$diff > 0, "HIGHER", "LOWER"),
        2^abs(tcyA_anc$diff))
```

> *Your answer:* does this support H1 or not?

## 6. Do your own test

Never trust a single tool. Re-do the comparison anc_TSB vs anc_SN yourself.

### 6a. A t-test on 3 vs 3

```{r ttest}
my_t_test <- function(key, data = abundances) {
  x <- filter(data, protein_key == key, group %in% c("anc_TSB", "anc_SN"))
  tsb <- x$normalized_abundance[x$group == "anc_TSB"]
  sn  <- x$normalized_abundance[x$group == "anc_SN"]
  welch <- t.test(tsb, sn)                    # unequal variances
  student <- t.test(tsb, sn, var.equal = TRUE)
  tibble(protein_key = key,
         mean_TSB = mean(tsb), mean_SN = mean(sn),
         diff_TSB_minus_SN = mean(tsb) - mean(sn),
         p_welch = welch$p.value, p_student = student$p.value)
}
own <- purrr::map(tcy$protein_key, my_t_test) |> bind_rows() |>
  left_join(select(tcy, protein_key, short_name), by = "protein_key") |>
  relocate(short_name)
own |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(v) signif(v, 3)))
```

**Question:** the t-test p-values are not adjusted for testing ~2300 proteins. Why
is that a problem? Why is that *less* of a problem here, where you test a
hypothesis you formulated *before* looking at the data?

### 6b. limma – borrowing information across proteins

With only 3 replicates the variance per protein is very uncertain. `limma`
shrinks each protein's variance towards the typical variance of all proteins
("moderated t-test"). prolfquapp does something similar.

```{r limma}
library(limma)
samples <- read_samples()
mat <- abundances |>
  select(protein_key, sample, normalized_abundance) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sample, values_from = normalized_abundance)
m <- as.matrix(mat[, samples$sample])         # columns in the order of the sample sheet
rownames(m) <- mat$protein_key

group  <- samples$group
design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + group)
colnames(design) <- levels(group)
fit <- lmFit(m, design)                         # proteins with NAs use their observed values
contr <- makeContrasts(TSB_vs_SN_at_anc = anc_TSB - anc_SN, levels = design)
fit2 <- eBayes(contrasts.fit(fit, contr))
limma_res <- topTable(fit2, number = Inf, sort.by = "none") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "protein_key") |>
  mutate(FDR_limma = p.adjust(P.Value, "BH"))

comparison <- tcy |>
  select(short_name, protein_key) |>
  left_join(select(own, protein_key, diff_ttest = diff_TSB_minus_SN, p_welch), by = "protein_key") |>
  left_join(select(limma_res, protein_key, diff_limma = logFC, p_limma = P.Value, FDR_limma),
            by = "protein_key") |>
  left_join(dea |> filter(contrast == "TSB_vs_SN_at_anc") |>
              select(protein_key, diff_prolfqua = diff, p_prolfqua = p.value, FDR_prolfqua = FDR),
            by = "protein_key") |>
  select(-protein_key)
comparison |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(v) signif(v, 3)))
```

**Questions:** Do the three methods agree on the *direction*? On the *size*? On
"significant or not"? Where do they differ, and why?

## 7. Effect size vs significance

```{r effect-size, fig.height=3.5}
dea |>
  filter(locus_tag %in% tcy$locus_tag, contrast == "TSB_vs_SN_at_anc") |>
  left_join(select(tcy, locus_tag, short_name), by = "locus_tag") |>
  ggplot(aes(diff, short_name)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high)) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 0.6, label = "higher in TSB ->", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.6, y = 0.6, label = "<- higher in SN", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "TSB_vs_SN_at_anc: log2 fold change with 95 % CI", y = NULL,
       title = "Ancestor, TSB vs SN")
```

For comparison: in the evolved *tcyA* frameshift mutant, TcyA dropped by
log2FC −5.95 (≈ 60-fold). Put your fold changes on the same scale.

**Questions:** A change can be *statistically significant* and still *tiny*.
Which is the case here? What would you need to call TcyABC "down-regulated"?

## 8. Your conclusion

> *Your answer:* Is H0 rejected? In which direction? Is the effect biologically
> relevant? How confident are you, and what are the caveats?

## 9. Discussion prompts

Discuss in your group (and write the outcome in your lab notebook):

1. **Plastic vs genetic response.** In *mSystems* the strong TcyA loss was a *genetic*
   effect (evolved frameshift vs ancestor). Here you look at the *plastic* effect of
   the medium in a non-evolved strain. Should those two agree? Why might a cell
   *not* down-regulate a transporter plastically even if losing it is adaptive?
2. **Operons and polar effects.** *tcyA, tcyB, tcyC* are co-transcribed. Do the three
   proteins move together here? Why did the frameshift in *tcyA* also reduce TcyB?
3. **Alternative routes.** Look at the L-cystine symporter (TcyP-like,
   `B7H15_02105`). What happens to it in SN? Could the cell compensate?
   `plot_protein("B7H15_02105")`
4. **Abundance ≠ activity.** A transporter can be present but closed, or
   inhibited by competition with other substrates. What experiment would measure
   *uptake* instead of protein amount?
5. **Nutrient depletion vs toxin defence.** SN = 70 % TSB + 30 % *spent*, cell-free
   *P. aeruginosa* medium. Spent medium is nutrient-poor – cystine/cysteine may be partly
   used up. Bacteria often *up*-regulate uptake systems when a nutrient becomes scarce.
   So a change in a transporter may reflect **nutrient availability** rather than
   **defence against secreted toxins**. Which experiment would separate the two
   (hint: TSB diluted with saline only; spent medium with cystine added back)?
6. **Short pulse.** Would you expect a change in protein amount after 15 min (SNpulse)?
